choices.text: The student is right - the bigger plate does the pushing
Nothing pushes it down: the cold, dense slab sinks under its own weight - slab-pull.
The oceanic plate is pushed down by ocean currents

questions.feedback: If you agreed with the student, that is the trap: The continental plate pushes the oceanic plate down underneath it. Reteach point: Nothing pushes it down: the cold, dense slab sinks under its own weight - slab-pull - and drags the rest of the plate behind it.
questions.misconception: The continental plate pushes the oceanic plate down underneath it.
questions.prompt: A student says the continental plate pushes the oceanic plate down underneath it. What is the best correction?

questions.answer: Oceanic plate rock is denser than continental plate rock, so at a convergent boundary the oceanic plate is the one that sinks.
questions.feedback: A strong answer names density as the deciding property - not size or strength.
questions.prompt: In one sentence, explain why the oceanic plate sinks rather than the continental plate.

choices.text: Only at the surface, in the ocean
Along the path of the sinking slab, as it cracks and grinds down
Inside the volcanoes of the arc
Nowhere - subduction is smooth and silent

questions.feedback: Scene 3 shows earthquakes tracking the slab downwards - they map the slab path.
questions.prompt: Where do earthquakes fire as the plate subducts?

questions.answer: The ocean trench forms where the plate bends down, and the rising magma builds a volcanic arc parallel to the trench.
questions.feedback: Credit trench plus volcanic arc, ideally with parallel to the trench.
questions.prompt: Name the surface feature where the plate bends down and the feature the rising magma builds.
